result.brief:
# Brief: Lecture slides "Filtragem / Restauração de Imagens" (45 pages, in Portuguese)

The slides are by Prof. Thiago Raposo Milhomem, Centro Universitário IESB. They are image-only, so everything below comes from rendering the pages. Many figures come from Gonzalez & Woods, Chapter 5 (Figs. 5.2, 5.5–5.8, 5.10, 5.13, 5.14, 5.16).

## 1. Filtering framework (pp. 4–6)
- **Spatial-domain filtering** (p. 4): a filter with impulse response (spatial mask) $h(x,y)$ is applied to the input $f(x,y)$, for example a noisy image. The output $g(x,y)$ is the processed (recovered) image: $g(x,y)=h(x,y)*f(x,y)$.
- **Fourier transform** (p. 5), the spatial-frequency domain: $F(u,v)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y)\,e^{-i2\pi(ux+vy)}\,dx\,dy$.
  - $f(x,y)$ is the spatial domain and $F(u,v)$ is the spatial-frequency domain.
  - $u$ is the frequency in the x direction and $v$ is the frequency in the y direction.
- **Convolution theorem** (p. 6): convolution in space equals a product in frequency, $G(u,v)=H(u,v)F(u,v)$.
  - $H$ is the frequency response of the filter (its Fourier spectrum).
  - $G$ and $F$ are the processed and input images in the frequency domain.
- **Degradation/restoration model** (pp. 7–8, identical slides): block diagram $f(x,y)\to$ degradation function $H$ $\to$ adder with noise $\eta(x,y)$ $\to g(x,y)\to$ restoration filter(s) $\to \hat f(x,y)$.
  - Spatial: $g(x,y)=h(x,y)*f(x,y)+n(x,y)$.
  - Frequency: $G(u,v)=H(u,v)F(u,v)+N(u,v)$.

The slide numbering of the framework slides is p. 4 (spatial), p. 5 (Fourier), p. 6 (frequency product) and pp. 7–8 (model). I confirmed this from the rendered order, in which the model slide appears twice.

## 2. Noise PDFs (pp. 9–15)
These use $z$ for gray level. Parameters are as printed on the slides.
- **Gaussian (p. 9):** $p(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-(z-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$.
- **Rayleigh (p. 9):** $p(z)=\frac{2}{b}(z-a)e^{-(z-a)^2/b}$ for $z\ge a$, and $0$ for $z<a$.
- **Erlang (p. 9):** $p(z)=\frac{a^b z^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}e^{-az}$ for $z\ge0$, and $0$ for $z<0$.
- **Uniform (p. 10):** $p(z)=\frac{1}{b-a}$ for $a\le z\le b$, and $0$ otherwise.
- **Exponential (p. 10):** $p(z)=ae^{-az}$ for $z\ge0$, and $0$ for $z<0$.
- **Impulsive (p. 10):** $p(z)=P_a$ at $z=a$, $P_b$ at $z=b$, and $0$ otherwise.
- **Fig. 5.2 diagrams (pp. 11–12):** six plots of $p(z)$ against $z$.
  - Gaussian: a bell curve centered at $\bar z$ with peak $1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)$. The height is $0.607/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)$ at $\bar z\pm\sigma$.
  - Rayleigh: starts at $a$ and peaks at $a+\sqrt{b/2}$ with height $0.607\sqrt{2/b}$.
  - Gamma/Erlang: peaks at $(b-1)/a$ with height $K=\frac{a(b-1)^{b-1}}{(b-1)!}e^{-(b-1)}$.
  - Exponential: decays from $a$ at $z=0$.
  - Uniform: a flat rectangle of height $1/(b-a)$ between $a$ and $b$.
  - Impulse: two spikes, $P_a$ at $a$ and $P_b$ at $b$.
- **Relabeled version (p. 12):** Gaussian is also called "Normal", Gamma is called "Erlang", and Impulse is called "Sal e Pimenta" (salt and pepper).
- **Worked visual example (pp. 13–15):**
  - The test image (p. 13) is a dark-gray square, a mid-gray inner square and a light circle, so its histogram has three modes.
  - p. 14 shows the noisy images and histograms for Gaussian, Rayleigh and Gamma noise. Each histogram has three peaks, each broadened or skewed by the noise type.
  - p. 15 shows Exponential, Uniform and Salt & Pepper. Exponential gives decaying humps and Uniform gives flat plateaus. Salt & Pepper gives isolated spikes at the extremes, with salt and pepper dots visible in the image.
  - No numeric parameters are given.

## 3. Restoration approaches (p. 16)
Restoration can use four kinds of analysis:
- spatial-domain analysis;
- frequency-domain analysis;
- known artifacts, "ruídos" conhecidos, such as 60.0 Hz;
- local statistics, meaning region-by-region analysis.

## 4. Periodic (sinusoidal) noise (pp. 17–18)
- **Fig. 5.5 (p. 17):** a lunar scene corrupted by sinusoidal noise. Its spectrum shows pairs of conjugate impulses, where each pair corresponds to one sine wave.
- **Fig. 5.16 (p. 18):** four panels.
  - (a) Corrupted image.
  - (b) Its spectrum.
  - (c) A Butterworth bandreject filter, drawn as a white disc-shaped region (value 1) with a dark ring (value 0).
  - (d) The clean restored image.

## 5. Local statistics (p. 19)
Fig. 5.6 shows histograms computed on small strips of the Gaussian, Rayleigh and uniform noisy images. The strip is shown as an inset. The point is that the noise PDF can be estimated from a flat region: bell-shaped, skewed, or flat.

## 6. Recap: spatial vs frequency filtering (pp. 20–21)
- Spatial: $g=h*f$. Frequency: $G=HF$.
- p. 21 adds a note that other transforms are also used, such as DCT and wavelets.

## 7. Example: DCT filtering on the Lena image (pp. 22–30)
- p. 22 shows the original image.
- p. 23 shows the DCT coefficients on the left. Energy is concentrated in the top-left corner, which is low frequency. On the right is a square window mask, white in the top-left and black elsewhere.
- Low-pass results with a square window of side $L$ keeping only the low-frequency coefficients:

| Page | L | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 24 | 150 | Slight blur |
| 25–26 | 100 | More blur; the slide repeats |
| 27 | 50 | Strong blur |
| 28 | 25 | Very blurred, with ringing |

- High-pass results are shown with $L=100$ (p. 29) and $L=25$ (p. 30). Edges and fine detail appear on a mostly black image, and larger detail appears for $L=25$.

## 8. Spatial filters from local statistics (pp. 31–33)
Here $S_{x,y}$ is the $m\times n$ neighborhood centered at $(x,y)$ and $g$ is the degraded image.
- **Arithmetic mean (p. 31):** $\hat f(x,y)=\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{(s,t)\in S_{xy}} g(s,t)$.
- **Median (p. 31):** $\hat f(x,y)=\operatorname{median}_{(s,t)\in S_{xy}} g(s,t)$.
- **Geometric mean (p. 31):** $\hat f(x,y)=\big[\prod_{(s,t)\in S_{xy}} g(s,t)\big]^{1/mn}$.
- **Harmonic mean (p. 32):** $\hat f(x,y)=\dfrac{mn}{\sum_{(s,t)\in S_{xy}} \frac{1}{g(s,t)}}$.
- **Contraharmonic mean (p. 32):** $\hat f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sum g(s,t)^{Q+1}}{\sum g(s,t)^{Q}}$, where $Q$ is the order of the filter.
- **Max and min (p. 32):** $\hat f=\max_{S_{xy}} g(s,t)$ and $\hat f=\min_{S_{xy}} g(s,t)$.
- **Midpoint (p. 33):** $\hat f(x,y)=\frac12\big[\max_{S_{xy}} g+\min_{S_{xy}} g\big]$.
- **Alpha-trimmed mean (p. 33):** $\hat f(x,y)=\frac{1}{mn-d}\sum_{S_{xy}} g(s,t)$. The $d/2$ lowest and $d/2$ highest values in the neighborhood are discarded. The slide writes $g(s,t)$ in the sum, but the sum is meant over the remaining values.

## 9. Worked examples on X-ray circuit-board images (pp. 34–40)
- **Fig. 5.7 (p. 34):** original, then additive Gaussian noise, then a $3\times3$ arithmetic mean and a $3\times3$ geometric mean. The geometric mean blurs slightly less.
- **Fig. 5.8 (p. 35):** pepper noise with probability 0.1 in (a), and salt noise with the same probability in (b).
  - (c) is (a) filtered with a $3\times3$ contraharmonic filter of order $Q=1.5$.
  - (d) is (b) filtered with $Q=-1.5$.
- **p. 36 rule:**
  - $Q>0$ removes pepper noise, and thins and blurs dark areas.
  - $Q<0$ removes salt noise, and thins and blurs light areas.
- **p. 37 wrong-sign example:** swapping the signs ($Q=-1.5$ on pepper, $Q=1.5$ on salt) makes the result much worse.
- **Fig. 5.10 (p. 38):** salt-and-pepper noise with $P_a=P_b=0.1$.
  - (b) is one pass of a $3\times3$ median filter.
  - (c) and (d) are the second and third passes. Residual noise falls with repeated passes.
- **p. 39:** $3\times3$ max and min filters applied to the noisy pepper and salt images. Annotations: the max filter reduces black details ("redução dos detalhes em preto") and the min filter reduces white details.
- **p. 40 comparison:** uniform noise, and uniform noise plus salt-and-pepper, filtered with mean, geometric mean, median and alpha-trimmed ($d=5$) filters. The visible conclusion is that the median and alpha-trimmed filters handle the mixed noise best.

## 10. Adaptive filters (pp. 41–44)
- **Adaptive mean/noise-reduction filter (p. 41):** the model is $g=f+n$. It uses the local variance $\sigma_L^2$, the local mean $\mu_L$, and the noise variance $\sigma_n^2$.
  - If $\sigma_n^2=0$, return $g(x,y)$.
  - If $\sigma_L^2\gg\sigma_n^2$ (an edge), return $g(x,y)$.
  - If the variances are close, return $\hat f(x,y)=g(x,y)-\frac{\sigma_n^2}{\sigma_L^2}\big(g(x,y)-\mu_L\big)$.
- **Adaptive median filter (p. 42):** notation:
  - $z_{min}$, $z_{max}$ and $z_{med}$ are the minimum, maximum and median gray level in $S_{xy}$.
  - $z_{xy}$ is the gray level at $(x,y)$.
  - $S_{max}$ is the maximum allowed window size.
  - **Level A:** compute $A1=z_{med}-z_{min}$ and $A2=z_{med}-z_{max}$.
    - If $A1>0$ and $A2<0$, go to Level B.
    - Otherwise increase the window size. If the window is still $\le S_{max}$, repeat Level A. If not, output $z_{xy}$.
  - **Level B:** compute $B1=z_{xy}-z_{min}$ and $B2=z_{xy}-z_{max}$.
    - If $B1>0$ and $B2<0$, output $z_{xy}$.
    - Otherwise output $z_{med}$.
- **Fig. 5.13 (p. 43):** Gaussian noise with zero mean and variance 1000. It compares arithmetic mean, geometric mean and adaptive noise-reduction filtering, all $7\times7$. The adaptive filter preserves edges best.
- **Fig. 5.14 (p. 44):** salt-and-pepper noise with $P_a=P_b=0.25$. It compares a $7\times7$ median filter with an adaptive median filter ($S_{max}=7$). The adaptive median keeps more detail.

## 11. Objective metrics (p. 45 and the end of the deck)
The deck is 45 pages, so the metrics slide is p. 45. My own page rendering placed the metrics slide at p. 42 of the second-to-last batch, and I could not fully reconcile the numbering of pp. 42–45 against the rendered batches. Treat the exact numbering of the last four slides as ±1. Their content is:
- **Relative error / MSE:** $MSE=\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big(X(i,j)-Y(i,j)\big)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big(X(i,j)\big)^2}$.
- **SNR:** $SNR_{dB}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1}{MSE}\right)$.
- **PSNR (peak SNR):** $PSNR_{dB}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{65025}{MSE}\right)$. Here $65025=255^2$.
- **CNR (contrast-to-noise ratio):** $CNR=\dfrac{\text{Medida de contraste}}{\text{Variância do ruído}}$.
- **SDR (signal-to-distortion ratio):** $SDR_{dB}=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1}{MSE}\right)$, equivalent to SNR.
- **Objective vs subjective quality:** an objective measure is not always consistent with perceived quality. Contrast, brightness, saturation and similar factors also affect subjective quality.
- **Final example:** the original Lena image, then two versions that both have PSNR of about 50 dB. One looks clean and the other is visibly noisy. This shows that PSNR alone can mislead.

## Prerequisites assumed from earlier lectures
- Convolution and spatial masks.
- The Fourier transform and the spectrum.
- Histograms and PDFs.
- Low-pass and high-pass filtering.
- The idea of the DCT (the title "Lembrando..." on pp. 20–21 signals a review of earlier material).
- The slides contain no explicit references to earlier lecture numbers.
